newsitem.title: USA: GFOA panel sets plan on defaulted book-entry munis.
newsitem.headline: GFOA panel sets plan on defaulted book-entry munis.

text.p: A GFOA panel on Saturday called on market groups to set uniform industry standards for promptly notifying investors in muni bonds that were registered via book entry whenever their bonds default.

"Owners of defaulted securities have not received important notices from issuers, registrars, paying agents or trustees that relate to the defaulted securities," the Government Finance Officers Association's governmental debt committee said at the association's annual conference here.

Bondholders are missing initial notices of a default, follow-up notices required by courts, and notices detailing developments in a case, like bond calls and tenders, the GFOA panel warned during a committee meeting on this and other issues.

The group's concerns stem from a 1982 federal law that required registration of ownership of newly issued municipal bonds and led to the demise of bearer bonds and physical delivery of new muni issues.

Many issuers adopted book-entry systems for registering bonds and directed registrars to register entire issues in the name of a securities depository, GFOA's panel said. Under most legal documents, notices are only required to be given to registered owners, the panel said.
As a result, many notices only go to nominees and do not reach the real, or "beneficial," owners of the bonds, the panel said.
The panel approved a two-page policy urging muni groups to develop uniform standards that ensure that important default notices get to the real bondholders.

The committee noted that the Securities and Exchange Commission has authority to mandate that market players contact the real bondholders. "However, GFOA prefers a voluntary effort by market participants," the committee said.
The panel stressed that the procedures are "not intended to create new disclosure obligations for issuers."

The committee listed 10 procedures. For instance, it said all nominees, regardless of their position in the chain of ownership, should "identify communications sent to them, transmit notices as required and assist issuers or their agents in providing the names and addresses of beneficial owners."
The panel also urged groups to set up procedures for paying "reasonable costs" whenever market players transmit notices.
GFOA's executive board is expected to adopt the policy at a vote scheduled for June 2. The group's general membership is set to vote on June 3.
